newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-UK threatens underwriters with MMC probe.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-UK threatens underwriters with MMC probe.

text.p: Britain's Office of Fair Trading (OFT) on Wednesday turned up the heat on underwriters of rights issues, with a threat to refer them to competition watchdog the Monopolies and Mergers Commission (MMC).
John Bridgeman, the director general of fair trading, said he was not satisfied there was sufficient commitment to open up the market for the underwriting of such issues.

His battle with the securities firms -- which underwrite rights issues for companies seeking to raise capital by issuing equity -- has been going on since 1995 and centres around the uniform fees charged by underwriters for their services.
He is also concerned about a potential conflict of interest where a company's financial adviser can also act as lead underwriter and broker for a rights issue.

"It is now up to the industry to decide whether to reform without such a reference or to subject itself to the full rigours of the MMC. I am not prepared to wait much longer for real and sustained evidence of a change," Bridgeman said.

Last December he called on underwriters to put their own house in order. But on Wednesday said he was continuing to monitor rights issues and warned that if markets proved incapable of reforming themselves he would take formal action.
Bridgeman said his aim had been to promote flexibility and competition in the market and he favoured non-intervention when possible.
And he questioned whether underwriting -- where a company is guaranteed the capital sum it wants to raise under a quick and well-rehearsed procedure -- was necessary in every case.
Bridgeman told a conference on new forms of corporate finance there should be more use of alternatives to underwriting, such as deep discounting and bookbuilding.

There has been a generally accepted standard charge of two percent of the capital raised by the underwriting financier. Bridgeman sees a deep-discount issue, where issues are priced attractively, as reducing costs.

Advisers have traditionally counselled an underwritten issue at a discount of between 10 and 15 percent of the company's current market price. But Bridgeman said this should be raised to a 30 or 40 percent discount, "making it extremely unlikely that the shares will not be taken up either by shareholders or in the open market".

If an adviser also went on to act as lead underwriter of an issue, it was "difficult to see financial advisers recommending a non-underwritten rights issue at a deep discount from the prevailing market price", despite this appearing to be the cheapest method, Bridgeman said.

Bridgeman said excessive costs of capital issues were at shareholders' expense but there was a further conflict of interest because sub-underwriters, who normally receive 1.25 percent, are frequently major shareholders in the company.
He said there had not been enough rights issues in the first quarter on which to base a decision on whether competition had increased.
But an analysis of 52 of the issues which were underwritten between June 1996 and the end of March 1997 did not auger well.
"The results show that sub-underwriting fees have only been marginally lower since the introduction of tendering and excess profits remain," Bridgeman said.

In October last year British investment bank Schroders Plc broke new ground in British institutional underwriting by using a tender within a 222 million pound ($368 million) rights issue for hotels group Stakis Plc.
This resulted in a reduced commission for Stakis, as the bank passed on pro-rata the reductions it achieved in the total sub-underwriting commissions.
Bridgeman said he was aware of 13 further rights issues where a proportion of the sub-underwriting had been put out to tender, in addition to five before December.

"If sub-underwriting had become truly competitive I would have expected to see a much greater variation in fees to reflect the risks. I would also have expected a significant reduction in excess returns," he added.
He said the structure of the tenders could also be more competitive. He said where tenders had been used, only a percentage of the underwriting had been tendered, diluting possible savings.
